A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Auto-Arena. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. Renamed and relocated material can be matched despite substantial revisions to the experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original English and Chinese tournaments, correlations with human preferences, peer-battle ablations, judge-agreement measurements, and behavioral case studies.

after.justification: v4 reports original tournament results and ablations, plus contamination analysis, a human study, and experiments comparing question sources and generators.

M1.justification: v4 Section 2.3 excludes judges from either participant's model family; v1's experimental setup excluded only the participants themselves. This refines committee selection. The three-stage framework, debate actions, prompt templates, reference-guided judging, and majority voting are retained.

E1.justification: The main English/Chinese coverage and eight question categories remain. Appendices C–D add focused scenarios involving benchmark web overlap, human identification of synthetic questions, and debates using math questions from MT-Bench, AMC-8, and AGI-Eval. These extend validation within otherwise retained domain coverage.

E2.justification: GPQA joins both principal benchmark comparisons. The new contamination comparison evaluates MMLU, ARC Challenge, and HellaSwag against generated questions. The existing principal comparators remain; v1's MT-Bench Hard and v4's Arena-Hard cite the same work and are matched as one comparator.

E3.justification: The primary/expanded English cohorts change from 7/17 to 9/15 models, with substantial roster changes. v4 adds individual-versus-majority-vote kappa measurements and new protocols using 100-question web-overlap samples, 30-versus-30 math-question comparisons, and two human raters. These substantially revise and extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained peer-battle ablation and behavioral examples, v4 adds a direct committee-discussion ablation, contamination checks, human and model comparisons of synthetic versus real questions, and a question-generator swap testing self-enhancement bias. Appendices C–E substantially broaden the questions tested about reliability and generalizability.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Bradley–Terry/Elo estimation is retained. New agreement comparisons and revised numerical values change evaluation endpoints and results, rather than uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: v1 reports 96.4%/94.5% correlations for its 7/17-model experiments; v4 reports 91.67%/92.14% for different 9/15-model cohorts. The strongest benchmark changes from LC-AlpacaEval to Arena-Hard in the primary comparison and MT-Bench after expansion. New results include 88.33% without committee discussions and 2%/28% contamination-proxy rates. These are revised or additional results, not same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: v4 makes the specified Swiss pairing count integer-valued, replacing log2(n) with ceil(log2(n)), and adds cost-scaling reasoning in Appendix H. No new theorems or proofs appear. Appendix H's nlog2(n) pairing count for adding one model conflicts with Section 4.1's logarithmic opponent count.

C1.justification: The central claims of fully automated evaluation, leading human-preference alignment, language adaptability, and competitive/learning behaviors remain. The introduction recalibrates headline evidence to 15 rather than 17 models, a 5-point rather than 46.4-point peer-battle benefit, and an 11-point rather than 20-point agreement increase.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands explanations of how decentralized follow-up questioning reduces generator bias and contamination concerns. Appendices C–E interpret question realism and generator-swap results, acknowledge unavailable training data behind the contamination proxy, and allow residual self-enhancement bias despite preserved rankings. These add substantive interpretations and qualifications beyond v1's design arguments.

D1.justification: v4 adds contamination-matching thresholds, sampling and volunteer details, model identifiers, selection reasons, licenses, and a $45 tournament/$5-per-model cost estimate. Existing prompts and length controls are retained. The direct code and leaderboard links supplied in v1 are omitted, while the project website remains and a demo link is added.

R1.justification: v4 expands research positioning through comparison matrices and citations covering evaluation surveys, GPQA, LLM-Eval, contamination detection, and synthetic evaluation data. It drops the ChatEval and WideDeep discussions and removes v1's assertion that prior multi-model evaluators lack collective discussion, refining the novelty positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and related work are extensively rewritten. v4 adds an explicit contribution list, moves related work near the end, separates leaderboard construction into its own section, combines component ablations, and reorganizes the appendices. These substantially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v4 redraws or reformats the overview, leaderboard plots, and retained behavioral illustrations. Correlation and ablation tables are consolidated, tables and figures increasingly use wrapped layouts, pairwise heatmaps move to Appendix F, and a new majority-vote agreement display appears. Several new comparison and analysis tables are added.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation through a direct committee-removal ablation and targeted contamination, question-realism, and generator-bias tests, addressing important evidentiary gaps in v1. Model-selection and cost documentation also improve transparency. The small math-focused studies and web-overlap proxy support limited conclusions, and model-count and cost-scaling inconsistencies remain, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in support for the framework's central claims.
